messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Actor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media Exposure: Related media content, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 52-year-old widowed American actor of Middle Eastern background who came to treatment after years of trying to keep himself functional by staying busy, staying around other people, and never letting his mind settle for too long. The trauma he returns to is the death of a loved one, an event he recounts in broken, visual flashes rather than as a smooth narrative. What comes back to him are pieces: a child crying somewhere nearby, a burst of sound he still cannot describe without tensing, a sequence of sharply lit images that sit in his mind like still photographs. He can see his loved one’s face, the angle of a doorway, the look of people who were supposed to be in charge, and then the memory breaks apart. He says there are gaps he cannot bridge, as if the worst day of his life exists in disconnected frames that refuse to become a whole story.

In the immediate aftermath, Nabil found himself seized not only by grief but by a sense that he had failed in a way he could never repair. He had come to believe that if he had acted differently, faster, more forcefully, the outcome might have changed. When he remembers the event, the guilt arrives instantly and with full force. He does not describe it abstractly; he feels it in his body, as though each image is an accusation. Alongside that is a bitter conviction that the people and institutions who should have protected his loved one did not do what they were meant to do, and that those responsible have faced no real consequences. He returns to this often, not as an argument but as a settled fact in his mind: the people who should have prevented it failed, and no one has been made to answer for that failure.

Over the months that followed, Nabil’s world became organized around the possibility of being caught off guard. He says that when other people tell him he is safe, the words do not land. He can hear them, but he cannot believe them. Strong fear, anger, guilt, and shame move through him quickly and without much warning, and his concentration has become unreliable enough that it interferes with his work. As an actor, he is expected to remain emotionally present, memorize lines, and tolerate long hours on sets where other people control the schedule, the soundscape, and the mood. He has found himself losing focus during table reads when a sound in the studio resembles something from that day, or when a scene involves distressed children and he hears crying that immediately pulls his attention away from the room in front of him. At times he has had to excuse himself after media interviews or promotional work because clips, news footage, or dramatized scenes related to harm and loss bring back those same hard-edged images. The reaction feels humiliating to him, especially in an industry where composure is expected and vulnerability can feel exposed.

His efforts to manage this have narrowed his life. Nabil avoids crowded places whenever he can. Shopping centers, public events, premieres, even busy restaurants feel unworkable, not because he simply dislikes them but because he cannot settle there; too much noise, too many people, too many unpredictable sounds. He also avoids being alone in a room or building. Even at home, solitude has become something he braces against. He leaves the television on, calls someone to come by, or arranges his day so that there is always another person nearby. On set, he has become known as unusually agreeable. He goes along with what directors, producers, or castmates want, even when he has preferences of his own, because yielding feels safer than risking friction or standing out. This habit has had costs. Colleagues experience him as easy to work with, but he feels increasingly absent from his own life, and he has taken roles, attended events, and stayed in situations longer than he wanted because saying no feels less safe than accommodating others.

What finally brought him to seek help was the sense that his life had become small and staged, even off camera. A recent encounter with related media content and the sound of children crying left him shaken enough that he struggled to get through work that week. He was troubled by how quickly his mind lost the present and returned to those photographic fragments. More than anything, he is frightened that this is permanent: that he will remain trapped between guilt over not doing more, certainty that those responsible will never be held accountable, and the impossibility of trusting that any place is truly safe. At the same time, he speaks with a quiet hope that if he can finally tell the story in a way that holds together, he might not have to keep arranging every part of his life around the next sound, the next image, or the fear of being left alone with his own mind.
